what_it_does: Every program uses a limited number of fast storage slots inside the processor called registers; the compiler's job of deciding which value goes in which register at each point in the program is called register allocation, and in the worst case it is provably as hard as solving a graph coloring puzzle (an NP-hard problem). In practice, compilers use rough heuristics that sometimes spill values to slower memory unnecessarily. This paper notices that real programs have a special structure — the graph of possible paths through the code (called a control-flow graph) is almost always narrow and tree-like, a property measured by a number called treewidth — and uses this to make the allocation problem much easier. By decomposing the control-flow graph into a tree-shaped structure and solving the allocation with dynamic programming on that tree, the algorithm's cost scales with treewidth rather than total program size, enabling near-optimal register allocation for the structured programs that appear in practice.
